inline.s: “If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land, after the end of their lives, were again to fall into the three evil destinies, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all possess bodies of true golden hue, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 03: Bodies of True Golden Color)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not all possess bodies of true golden hue, then may I not become a Buddha.
[All]
entirely.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should differ in form and color and have the fair and the ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 04: Neither Fair nor Ugly)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land differed in form and color and had the fair and the ugly, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Fair and ugly] Good and not good. Here “ugly” means that a thing is not good, as in “ugly field.” [Have the fair and the ugly] Having distinctions of good and not good.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the power of knowing past lives, down to knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 05: The Power of Knowing Past Lives)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the power of knowing past lives, down to knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Nayuta] The name of a number, equal to what is now called a koti.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine eye, down to seeing a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 06: The Power of the Divine Eye)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the divine eye, down to seeing a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine ear, down to hearing all that a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddhas have spoken and receiving and upholding it all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 07: The Power of the Divine Ear)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the divine ear, down to hearing all that a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddhas have spoken and receiving and upholding it all, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the knowledge of others’ minds, down to knowing the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 08: The Power of Knowing Others’ Minds)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the knowledge of others’ minds, down to knowing the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they cannot go beyond a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 09: The Unobstructed Power of Travel)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they cannot go beyond a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts and be covetous of and calculating about their bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 10: No Coveting or Calculating about the Body)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land gave rise to thoughts and were covetous of and calculating about their bodies, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Covetous of and calculating about the body] Falsely clinging to a self and a body (falling into the view of a body) and, with greed, calculating and measuring love and hate, compliance and opposition, and the like. Ordinary people in cultivation mostly fall into the view of a body, and the view of a body stands first among the delusions of view; if the delusions of view are not cut off, one cannot enter the stream of the sages. [Delusions of view] The delusions of view are the errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a body, extreme views, evil views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and observances.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not abide in the certain state and must reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 11: Abiding in the Right and Certain State)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not abide in the right and certain state and must reach nirvana, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Certain state] An abbreviation of “the right and certain state.” [The three groups] The three groups are three classes of beings: the right and certain group (abbreviated as the certain group), the wrong and certain group, and the uncertain group. The right and certain group refers to the class of beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the wrong and certain group refers to the class of beings who in the end cannot realize enlightenment; the uncertain group refers to the class of beings between right and wrong, who may or may not realize enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light should be measurable, down to not shining upon a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 12: Immeasurable Light)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and my light were limited, down to not shining upon a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan should be measurable, down to a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 13: The Buddha’s Immeasurable Life)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and my lifespan were limited, down to a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sravakas in my land should be countless, so that even if the beings of a trichiliocosm all became pratyekabuddhas and together calculated for a hundred thousand kalpas, they could know their number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 14: Countless Sravakas)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the sravakas in my land were countless, so that even if the beings of a trichiliocosm all became pratyekabuddhas and together calculated for a hundred thousand kalpas, they could know their number, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land should be beyond measure. Except that, by their original vows, they may make it long or short
as they wish. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 15: The Measureless Lifespans of the Beings)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land were without limit, except that, by their original vows, they may make it long or short as they wish; if it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[If it were not so] If it were not thus.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should so much as hear of any evil name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 16: Hearing No Evil Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land so much as heard of any evil name, then may I not become a Buddha.
so much as hear of any evil name
] In the Land of Ultimate Bliss not even the name of evil exists, so how could there be evil deeds? To such a degree does the surpassing excellence of the Land of Ultimate Bliss reach!
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countless Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions should not all praise and proclaim my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 17: Praise by All the Buddhas)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the countless Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions did not all praise and proclaim my name, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, desire to be born in my land, and even for ten thoughts, should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Only those who have committed the five rebellious acts and slandered the right Dharma are excepted.
(Vow 18: Certain Rebirth through Ten Thoughts)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, desire to be born in my land, and even for ten thoughts, should not be born there, then may I not become a Buddha. Only those who have committed the five rebellious acts and slandered the right Dharma are excepted.

[Utmost sincerity] A heart utterly sincere and utterly firm. [Even for ten thoughts] This is an abbreviated way of saying “even at the point of death, with ten thoughts in unbroken succession, invoking my name.” As to the precise meaning of “even for ten thoughts” in the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo teaches in the Collection of the Land of Peace:
“If there are beings who, though they have done evil all their lives,
at the time of death, with ten thoughts in unbroken succession, invoke my name
, and should they not be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(For details, see
“Even for Ten Thoughts”
“The Eighteenth Vow”
) [Ten thoughts in unbroken succession] Without admixture of false thoughts, invoking the name of Amitabha ten times with mind succeeding mind. Master Tanluan teaches:
“With no other mind intermingled
(without admixture of false thoughts)
, mind succeeding mind
(mind following upon mind
, even for ten thoughts, this is called ten thoughts in unbroken succession.”
He also says:
“Ten thoughts in unbroken succession at the point of death, and one attains rebirth.”
(For details, see
“Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teaching”

) [The five rebellious acts] Five kinds of offenses that run utterly counter to principle: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the Buddha’s blood, and causing division in the Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, and because committing any one of them brings a fall into the Avici Hell, they are also called “uninterrupted karma.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who have aroused the bodhi mind and cultivated all merits, and who with utmost sincerity make vows and desire to be born in my land, should at the end of their lives not be met and surrounded by a great assembly appearing before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 19: Rebirth through Utmost Sincerity)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the ten directions who have aroused the bodhi mind and cultivated all merits, and who with utmost sincerity make vows and desire to be born in my land, should at the end of their lives not be met and surrounded by a great assembly appearing before them, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, are mindful of my land, plant the roots of all virtues, and with utmost sincerity dedicate them, desiring to be born in my land, should not have their wish fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 20: Certain Rebirth through Mindfulness)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, are mindful of my land, plant the roots of all virtues, and with utmost sincerity dedicate them, desiring to be born in my land,
should not have their wish fulfilled
, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Roots of virtue] That is to say, roots of goodness. Virtue means goodness; root means foundation. The merit of all good practices is the foundation of the fruition of Buddhahood. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Before all the Buddhas, they planted the roots of all virtues.”
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:
“They extinguished all outflows and planted the roots of all virtues.”

[Dedication] “Turning one’s own roots of virtue toward a certain goal”: concentrating and directing the roots of virtue one has created toward some purpose, so that it may be quickly accomplished. For example, one dedicates all the good one has cultivated through the three karmas (bodily, verbal, and mental), and even such merits as repentance and entreaty, to all beings of the Dharma realm, that they may together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
“Dedication means turning one’s own merit and giving it universally to beings, that together they may see the Tathagata Amitabha and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Shandao’s Verses on Arousing the Vow and Taking Refuge in the Three Treasures say:
“May this merit of mine be given equally to all, that together we may arouse the bodhi mind and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
(The Liturgy of the Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 21: The Thirty-Two Marks)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The thirty-two marks of a great man] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great man: 1. level soles; 2. wheels with a thousand spokes on the soles; 3. long, slender fingers; 4. soft hands and feet; 5. webbed hands and feet; 6. full and rounded heels; 7. high and well-formed insteps; 8. calves (
shuàn

) like those of a royal deer; 9. hands reaching past the knees; 10. the pudendum concealed like that of a horse; 11. breadth and length of body; 12. blue-black hair pores; 13. body hair curling upward; 14. a golden body; 15. a constant light of ten feet; 16. fine, smooth skin; 17. the seven places full and rounded; 18. full armpits; 19. a body like a lion; 20. an upright body; 21. full and rounded shoulders; 22. forty teeth in the mouth; 23. teeth white, even, and close-set;

24. four teeth pure white; 25. jawbones (the palate bones that hold the teeth) like those of a lion; 26. the fluids of the throat attaining the finest flavor; 27. a broad, long tongue; 28. a pure, far-reaching Brahma voice; 29. dark blue eyes; 30. eyelashes like those of a royal bull; 31. a white tuft between the eyebrows; 32. a fleshy mound on the crown of the head. [Dark blue (
gàn
)] A color black with red showing through.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land should not ultimately reach the stage of one life to Buddhahood; except that, by their original vows, for the sake of beings they don the armor of their vast vows and go to other worlds, freely delivering all. Roaming through all Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulating the roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathagatas of the ten directions. Teaching and transforming beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way,
transcending the practices of the ordinary stages
and manifesting the cultivation of the virtue of Samantabhadra. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 22: One Life to Buddhahood)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land should not ultimately reach the stage of one life to Buddhahood; except that, by their original vows, for the sake of beings they don the armor of their vast vows and go to other worlds, freely delivering all beings. Roaming through all Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulating the roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathagatas of the ten directions. And they teach and transform beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way, transcending the practices of the ordinary stages and manifesting the cultivation of the virtue of Samantabhadra. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[One life to Buddhahood] Filling the Buddha’s place when this one life ends: this is another name for the bodhisattva of the last body (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment). For example, Maitreya Bodhisattva, who now dwells in the inner court of the Tusita Heaven, is a bodhisattva of one life to Buddhahood. All the beings who attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable lifespans and attain Buddhahood in this one life; the “one life” spoken of refers to one life of segmentary birth-and-death. But the “one life” in “filling the Buddha’s place when this one life ends” refers to one life of transformation birth-and-death. [Donning the armor of their vast vows] They don the great armor adorned by the merit of their vast vows. [Causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way] Teaching and transforming them to cultivate the Pure Land Dharma-gate. “The unsurpassed, right, and true way”

refers to the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Because the Pure Land Dharma-gate is perfect and direct, expedient and ultimate, a single leap that goes straight in, the most perfect and sudden of all, it is called the unsurpassed, right, and true way. Master Hanshan teaches:

“The one gate of the Pure Land embraces all three capacities alike, and the sudden and the gradual enter together; there is no capacity it does not gather in. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms sideways,
and it is the most supreme Dharma-gate
He also teaches:
“The Buddha spoke of many expedient gates for cultivating the way out of birth and death, but only reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land
is the most swift and essential
(Dream-Play Collection
Preface to Pointing the Way Home to the Pure Land)

[Transcending the practices of the ordinary stages] Surpassing the cultivation of the common path, in which one advances stage by stage in fixed order. In cultivation on the common path, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages from ordinary being to Buddhahood, namely: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten stages of ground, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. But one who cultivates the Pure Land Dharma-gate and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss sees the Buddha when the flower opens, awakens to the non-arising, and obtains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, ascending to the eighth ground. [The eighth ground] The eighth of the bodhisattva’s ten grounds, called the Ground of Immovability. On this ground the bodhisattva abides in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, cuts off all exertion, and puts body and mind to rest, like empty space; he accomplishes the perfection of vow and, with a mind of nirvana, is still and unmoving, and so it is called the “Ground of Immovability.” [The ten grounds] The Ground of Joy, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulties, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Reaching, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud. These are the fifth of the ten sets in the bodhisattva’s fifty-two stages of cultivation. On these ten grounds one gradually opens the realm of Buddhahood and accomplishes the wisdom of all modes; they already belong to the stage of the sages, and so they are also called the “ten sages.” [The three wisdoms] The wisdom of all, the wisdom of the paths, and the wisdom of all modes. The wisdom of all is the wisdom by which sravakas and pratyekabuddhas understand the general characteristic of all dharmas, the general characteristic being the true nature of all dharmas; the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom by which bodhisattvas understand the various gates of practice; the wisdom of all modes is the wisdom by which the Buddha comprehends both the general and the particular characteristics of all dharmas and, teaching and cutting off delusion, transforms beings.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, should make offerings to all Buddhas and, in the space of a single meal, be unable to reach a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 23: Making Offerings to All Buddhas)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, made offerings to all Buddhas and, in the space of a single meal, were unable to reach a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The space of a single meal] The time of one meal. The Perfection of Wisdom Sutra
Fascicle 347

Chapter of Entrustment arranges lengths of time in order: one day and night, one day, half a day, one hour (equal to two hours today), the space of a meal, a moment, an instant, the space of a breath.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, presenting the roots of virtue before all Buddhas, should not obtain the offerings they require as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 24: Offerings as They Wish)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land, presenting the roots of virtue (roots of goodness) before all Buddhas, should not obtain the offerings they require as they wish, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Offerings] Also called offerings. Things such as incense, flowers, food and drink, banners, and canopies offered to Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Ratnakuta Sutra says:
“Bearing
(jī, to carry)
wondrous offerings, they present them to the Tathagata and the great assembly.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“In ages to come, with all manner of offerings, they will make offerings and serve.”
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should be unable to expound the wisdom of all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 25: Expounding the Wondrous Wisdom)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land were unable to expound the wisdom of all, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The wisdom of all] The wisdom that understands the general characteristic of all dharmas, the general characteristic being the true nature of all dharmas.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain bodies of vajra Narayana, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 26: The Body of Narayana)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land did not obtain bodies of vajra Narayana, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The body of vajra Narayana] A body as solid as vajra and with strength as measureless as that of the god Narayana; hence it is called the body of vajra Narayana.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, all the myriad things of the devas and humans in my land should not be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, with forms and colors most extraordinary, reaching the subtle and the ultimate, beyond all reckoning; and if any being there, even one who has attained the divine eye, should be able to discern and distinguish their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 27: All Adorned and Pure)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and all the myriad things of the devas and humans in my land were not adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, with forms and colors most extraordinary, reaching the subtle and the ultimate, beyond all reckoning; and if any being in my land, even one who has attained the divine eye, should be able to discern and distinguish their names and numbers, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Names and numbers]
The number of the items.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of scant merit, should be unable to know and see the bodhi tree of that land, with its immeasurable light and color and its height of four million li, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 28: Knowing and Seeing the Bodhi Tree)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of scant merit, were unable to know and see the bodhi tree of that land, with its immeasurable light and color and its height of four million li, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and expound the sutras and Dharma should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 29: Wisdom through Reciting the Sutras)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and expound the sutras and Dharma did not obtain eloquence and wisdom, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land should be measurable, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 30: Unmeasurable Wisdom and Eloquence)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land were measurable, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the land should not be pure and should not reflect and reveal all the measureless, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as a bright mirror reveals the face. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 31: Revealing the Ten Directions)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the land were not pure and did not reflect and reveal all the measureless, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground upward and up to the sky, the palaces, towers, terraces, pools, streams, flowers, and trees, all the myriad things in my land, should not be formed in common from measureless jewels and fragrances. Adorned and wondrous, surpassing all devas and humans. Their fragrance pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the practices of the Buddha. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 32: The Wondrous Adornment of Jewel Fragrance)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and from the ground upward and up to the sky, the palaces, towers, terraces, pools, streams, flowers, and trees, all the myriad things in my land, were not formed in common from measureless jewels and fragrances. Adorned and wondrous, surpassing all devas and humans. Their fragrance pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the practices of the Buddha. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions whose bodies are touched by my light should not be supple in body and mind, surpassing devas and humans, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 33: Supple Bodies upon Touching the Light)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions whose bodies are touched by my light were not supple in body and mind, surpassing devas and humans. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not obtain the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and the profound dharani, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 34: Attaining Patience upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name did not obtain the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and the profound dharani, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising: penetrating the truth that all dharmas are originally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are empty just as they are; and therefore abiding in the non-arising without the mind stirring. [No nature of their own] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial reality (and so are illusory), and this is called having no nature of their own. The Lotus Sutra says:
“One knows that all dharmas are always without a nature of their own.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All illusions are accomplished as without a nature of their own.”
[Dharani]
Holding all dharmas, so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, I cause there to be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and even flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 35: No Women, Born in Lotuses)
“If I were to become a Buddha

I would cause there to be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and even flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[I cause there to be no women in my land]
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitabha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Deliverance of Human Beings (the Wu Translation) says:

“The second vow: when I attain Buddhahood, may there be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools of water. When grown they are all bodhisattvas and arhats, countless in number. If I obtain this vow, then I shall attain Buddhahood; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never attain Buddhahood.”
[Countless] Without end.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas in the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the way of Buddhahood. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 36: Always Cultivating Pure Conduct)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas in the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the way of Buddhahood. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Pure conduct]
Pure and clean action.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should bow with all five limbs to the ground, pay homage with head bowed, rejoice, have faith, and delight in cultivating the bodhisattva path, so that devas and humans of the world all pay them reverence. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 37: Homage by Devas and Humans)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should bow with all five limbs to the ground, pay homage with head bowed, rejoice, have faith, and delight in cultivating the bodhisattva path, so that devas and humans of the world all pay them reverence. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land, wishing to obtain clothing, should have it arrive as soon as they think of it. Wondrous robes praised by the Buddha and in accord with the Dharma should naturally be on their bodies. If there were any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 38: Wondrous Robes upon Thought)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land, wishing to obtain clothing, had it arrive as soon as they thought of it, with wondrous robes praised by the Buddha and in accord with the Dharma naturally on their bodies. If there were any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not enjoy bliss equal to that of a bhiksu who has exhausted the outflows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 39: Bliss Like the Exhaustion of Outflows)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not enjoy bliss equal to that of a bhiksu who has exhausted the outflows, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Exhaustion of outflows] The complete cutting off of all afflictions (the delusions of view and of thought). Outflow is another name for affliction. [The delusions of view and of thought] The delusions of view and the delusions of thought. The delusions of view are the errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a body, extreme views, evil views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and observances; the delusions of thought are the errors of ordinary people in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of the beings’ revolving in birth and death; cut them off, and one can end birth and death and escape the round.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who wish, as they please, to see the measureless, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, should have their wish fulfilled at once and see them all reflected in the jeweled trees, as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 40: Revealing the Lands in the Trees)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land who wish, as they please, to see the measureless, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, had their wish fulfilled at once and saw them all reflected in the jeweled trees, as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should until they attain Buddhahood have deficient or imperfect faculties, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 41: Faculties Without Deficiency)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should until they attain Buddhahood have deficient or imperfect faculties, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should all obtain the samadhi of purity and liberation. Abiding in this samadhi, in the space of a single thought of intent, they make offerings to measureless, inconceivable World-Honored Buddhas without losing their concentration. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 42: Abiding in Samadhi and Making Offerings)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, all obtained the samadhi of purity and liberation. Abiding in this samadhi, in the space of a single thought of intent, they make offerings to measureless, inconceivable World-Honored Buddhas without losing their concentration. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives be born into honored and noble families. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 43: Merit upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives be born into honored and noble families. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should rejoice and leap for joy, cultivate the bodhisattva path, and be complete in the roots of virtue. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 44: Complete in the Roots of Virtue)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, rejoiced and leaped for joy, cultivated the bodhisattva path, and were complete in the roots of virtue (roots of goodness). If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should all obtain the universal and equal samadhi. Abiding in this samadhi, until they attain Buddhahood they always see all the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 45: The Universal and Equal Samadhi)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, all obtained the universal and equal samadhi. Abiding in this samadhi, until they attain Buddhahood they always see all the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The universal and equal samadhi] One who cultivates this meditative concentration can see all Buddhas within the concentration.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows and aspirations, should not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 46: Hearing the Dharma as Vowed)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows and aspirations, did not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should not immediately attain non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 47: Non-Retrogression upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, did not immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The stage of non-retrogression] Also written Avaivartika, or A-pi (
pí

) pa-chih. This is the name of a stage of the bodhisattva, which a bodhisattva can reach only after cultivating for one great asamkhyeya kalpa. From that point on there is only advance step by step until Buddhahood, with no retrogression in between. The Amitabha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:
“In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all beings who are born there are Avaivartika.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should not immediately attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 48: Attaining the Three Patient Acceptances)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, did not immediately attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma were unable immediately to attain non-retrogression, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The first, second, and third patient acceptances] Namely the patience of sound, the patience of compliance, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. For the explanations of these three kinds of patience, see in detail “Fifteen, The Place of Enlightenment.”
“The Buddha said to Ananda: At that time, when Dharmakara Bhiksu had spoken these vows, he spoke in verse:
I founded a resolve surpassing the world, and I shall surely reach the unsurpassed Way
(I shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood)
, and if these vows are not fulfilled
(if these forty-eight vows are not fulfilled)
, I vow not to attain equal enlightenment
(I vow not to become a Buddha)
